title: The Making of a Boy
subtitle: New York, 1858–1880
intro: Asthma nearly killed him before he was ten. He built a museum in his bedroom, learned to mount his own specimens, and did what his father told him to do about his body. Fifteen questions on the years before anyone had heard of Theodore Roosevelt.

heroCredit: "Teedie" at about two years old. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What was Theodore Roosevelt's childhood nickname?
questions.explanation: The family called him "Teedie." His father was "Thee," and his eldest son would later be "Ted." He disliked "Teddy" all his life — that one was the public's invention, not his family's.
questions.imageAlt: Carte-de-visite portrait of Theodore Roosevelt at about two years old
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, about two years old. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

link.label: More on the name he hated

questions.prompt: Where was Roosevelt born on October 27, 1858?
options: A brownstone at 28 East 20th Street, Manhattan
The Roosevelt mansion on Union Square
His grandfather's estate on the Hudson
questions.explanation: A five-storey brownstone at 28 East 20th Street, in what was then a fashionable stretch of Manhattan. The house was demolished in 1916 and rebuilt as a memorial after his death; it stands today as the Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt's birthplace at 28 East 20th Street, New York
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt's birthplace, 28 East 20th Street, New York. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.explanation: Asthma, and the medicine of the 1860s had almost nothing to offer. Among the remedies tried were strong black coffee — which, as it happens, was a sound guess, since caffeine is chemically close to the theophylline later used to treat asthma — and, on one bad night at sea, a cigar administered by his father.
questions.imageAlt: Tintype of the four Roosevelt children
questions.credit: The Roosevelt children. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's father gave him an instruction that shaped the rest of his life. What was it?
options: That he must make his name
That he must make his fortune
That he must make his peace
That he must make his body
questions.explanation: Theodore Roosevelt Sr. told his frail son that he had the mind but not the body, and that without the help of the body the mind could not go as far as it should. "You must make your body." The boy set to work in a gymnasium his father fitted out on the second-floor piazza.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt as a young boy
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, about two years old. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

link.label: The man who shaped a president

questions.prompt: What started Roosevelt's lifelong interest in natural history?
options: A gift of Audubon's Birds of America
A dead seal laid out in a Broadway market
A visit to the London Zoo
A hawk he watched from his bedroom window
questions.explanation: He was sent out for strawberries and came across a dead seal on a slab of wood in a Broadway market. He measured it obsessively, got hold of the skull, and made it the first specimen of the grandly named "Roosevelt Museum of Natural History" — an institution he founded with two cousins, complete with its own labels.
questions.imageAlt: The Roosevelt children photographed as a tintype
questions.credit: The Roosevelt children. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

link.label: Building a museum in his bedroom

questions.prompt: Who taught the young Roosevelt taxidermy?
questions.explanation: John G. Bell kept a taxidermy shop on Broadway and had travelled west with Audubon himself. Roosevelt took lessons there as a boy. It was practical training, not a hobby: he mounted his own specimens for years, and some of them ended up in the Smithsonian.
questions.credit: The Roosevelt children. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: At about thirteen, Roosevelt discovered something that he said "literally opened an entirely new world to me." What was it?
options: His first visit to the American Museum of Natural History
questions.explanation: He had realised his companions could see things he could not — and read signboards he could only guess at. He told his father, and got spectacles. In his Autobiography he wrote that they "literally opened an entirely new world to me." He had been badly near-sighted for years without anyone noticing.
questions.imageAlt: The Roosevelt children and companions photographed in Dresden
questions.credit: Dresden Literary American Club. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

link.label: Ten facts about T.R.'s early life

questions.prompt: What historic event did the six-year-old Roosevelt watch from a window of his grandfather's house on Union Square?
options: The return of the Union army
questions.explanation: On April 25, 1865, Lincoln's funeral procession moved up Broadway past the Roosevelt house near Union Square, church bells tolling. A photograph taken that day shows two small boys at an upstairs window — believed to be Theodore and his brother Elliott.
questions.imageAlt: The New York house where Theodore Roosevelt was born
questions.credit: "Where Teddy was born." Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: The Roosevelt household was divided by the Civil War. How?
options: His grandfather bankrolled regiments on both sides
His mother's family served the Confederacy
His father fought for the Confederacy
His parents were estranged over abolition
questions.explanation: Theodore Sr. stood with the Union. Mittie Bulloch Roosevelt was a Georgian: her half-brother James Bulloch built the Confederate raider Alabama, and her younger brother Irvine served aboard it. The contradiction lived in the family parlour throughout the war. Theodore Sr. did not fight either — out of deference to his Southern wife he hired a substitute, as the law then allowed, and spent the war as an Allotment Commissioner, persuading soldiers to send their pay home to their families. It was honourable work and it was not the front, and his son grew up conscious of the difference.
questions.imageAlt: Alice, Corinne and Anna Roosevelt photographed together
questions.credit: Alice, Corinne, and Anna. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt had three siblings. Which of these was NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: Bamie, Elliott and Corinne. Emlen was a cousin. Bamie became the most trusted confidante of Theodore's life and would raise his daughter Alice after 1884. Elliott, charming and headed for tragedy, was the father of Eleanor Roosevelt.
questions.imageAlt: Alice Lee Roosevelt, Corinne Roosevelt and Anna Roosevelt
questions.credit: Alice, Corinne, and Anna. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's younger brother Elliott is remembered today largely as whose father?
questions.explanation: Elliott was Eleanor Roosevelt's father. In 1884 the two brothers each had a daughter — Theodore's Alice and Elliott's Eleanor. Eleanor would later marry a distant cousin, Franklin, and it was Uncle Theodore who gave her away.
questions.imageAlt: Elliott and Theodore Roosevelt photographed in hunting outfits
questions.credit: Elliott and Theodore Roosevelt in hunting outfits. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How did Roosevelt prepare for Harvard, having never attended a conventional school?
questions.explanation: His schooling had been irregular — travel, illness, and tutors at home. In 1873 the family hired Arthur Cutler, a young Harvard graduate, to drill him for the entrance examinations. The preparation was rigorous and it worked: he passed and entered Harvard in the autumn of 1876.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt children and companions in Dresden
questions.credit: Dresden Literary American Club. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: In the late summer of 1880, weeks after leaving Harvard, Roosevelt went west with his brother Elliott. To do what?
options: Shoot birds across Illinois, Iowa and Minnesota
Report on the Adirondack lumber camps for a magazine
Walk the length of the Erie Canal
questions.explanation: A hunting trip that ran for weeks, ending at Moorhead on the Red River, at the edge of what was then unorganised Dakota Territory. Between them the brothers brought down 404 birds — grouse, snipe, plover, geese — and Theodore kept a tally, finishing two ahead of Elliott, which mattered to him more than it should have. His asthma was bad out there and some nights he had to sleep sitting up. It was his first sight of the big country west of Chicago, and he came home talking about the size of it.
questions.imageAlt: Elliott and Theodore Roosevelt photographed standing in hunting outfits
questions.credit: Elliott and Theodore Roosevelt in hunting outfits, photographed by H. Rocher at Chicago in the summer of 1880 — at the start of this trip. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What happened in February 1878, during Roosevelt's sophomore year?
options: He suffered his last major asthma attack
questions.explanation: Theodore Roosevelt Sr. died of a stomach tumour, aged forty-six. His son marked the date beside a verse of the 69th Psalm in his Bible. He had worshipped his father, and called him the best man he ever knew; the loss reshaped what he thought he owed the world.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt photographed as a college student
questions.credit: "Theo. Roosevelt at college." Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt married Alice Hathaway Lee on October 27, 1880. What else was that day?
questions.explanation: His twenty-second birthday. They were married in the Unitarian church at Brookline, Massachusetts. He had pursued her relentlessly for two years. She would die four years later, hours after their daughter was born and in the same house as his mother.
questions.imageAlt: Alice Hathaway Lee, the first Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt
questions.credit: The first Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt (Alice Hathaway Lee). Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.
